title: Public Key Encryption Secure Against Quantum Leakage
authors: Alper Cakan, Fuyuki Kitagawa, Ryo Nishimaki, Manasi Shingane, and Takashi Yamakawa
abstract:
Side-channel attacks are a relevant threat to many modern cryptographic schemes and often have fatal consequences such as revealing partial information about secret keys. While leakage-resilient cryptography aims to solve this problem, existing works focus exclusively on showing security against classical leakage. Moreover, recent public key encryption (PKE) schemes utilizing quantum secret keys achieve security against unbounded classical leakage, but offer no guarantees on any amount of quantum leakage. Since security guarantees on classical side information do not necessarily translate to guarantees on quantum side information, showing PKE schemes that are secure in the presence of quantum leakage remains open. 

    In this work, we address this problem by extending the definition of leakage resilience for PKE in the bounded-leakage model to allow for quantum leakage. We provide the following two constructions:
        - PKE with Quantum Secret Keys: We construct a PKE scheme that tolerates unbounded classical leakage alongside bounded, constant-rate ($\lambda <0.057$) quantum leakage. Our construction assumes the existence of polynomially secure post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) as well as one-way functions (OWFs). 
      - PKE with Classical Secret Keys: We construct a classical PKE scheme that is secure against bounded quantum leakage. Our construction offers a tradeoff between the achievable leakage rate and the underlying cryptographic assumptions. Assuming the hardness of the learning with errors problem (LWE) we obtain an optimal leakage rate of $\lambda \leq 1-o(1)$. Alternatively, assuming only post-quantum PKE, we obtain a leakge rate of $\lambda\leq \frac{1}{poly(n)}$.

1        Introduction
Modern cryptographic schemes are often deployed in environments where secret keys may not re-
main perfectly hidden. Partial information about a secret key can be exposed through side-channel
attacks, compromised randomness, or timing attacks. Leakage-resilient cryptography [ISW03,
MR04, DP08] studies the extent to which such leakage can be tolerated while preserving the security
of the underlying scheme.
    In the public key setting, leakage-resilient public key encryption (PKE) has been studied under
a variety of leakage models, including bounded leakage model [AGV09, NS09, HLWW16], bounded

retrieval model [DLW06, Dzi06, ADW09], auxiliary-input leakage model [DKL09], and continual
leakage model [BKKV10, DHLW10]. Among these models, the bounded leakage model is the most
relevant to this work. In this model, the number of leakage bits that an adversary can obtain from
the secret key is bounded. This bound is necessary for meaningful security: without such a bound,
the entire secret key could be leaked, in which case security is trivially impossible.
    Interestingly, a recent work of Çakan, Goyal, Liu-Zhang, and Ribeiro [ÇGLZR24] shows that this
seemingly unavoidable barrier in the bounded-leakage model can be overcome if one uses quantum
secret keys while allowing only classical leakage. In this setting, the trivial attack of leaking the
entire secret key is ruled out, since a quantum secret key cannot in general be fully encoded as
classical leakage.
    They construct a PKE scheme with quantum secret keys that tolerates unbounded classical
leakage, building on earlier techniques for PKE with copy-protected secret keys (a.k.a. single-
decryptor encryption) [CLLZ21]. A caveat of their construction, however, is that it offers no security
guarantee in the presence of quantum leakage. This is a natural concern once the secret key itself
is quantum: a compromised implementation may expose part of the quantum register holding the
secret key, rather than merely producing classical side information about it. For example, quantum
leakage could correspond to a certain fraction of the qubits of the secret key becoming public.
Ideally, one would like to have guarantees on how much of the quantum secret key can be leaked
while still preserving the security of the underlying scheme. Of course, it is impossible to tolerate
unbounded quantum leakage: if the entire secret key is leaked, security is impossible. Nevertheless,
it may still be possible to achieve security against bounded quantum leakage.
    This motivates the following natural question:
  Can we construct a PKE scheme with quantum secret keys that tolerates unbounded classical
                          leakage and bounded quantum leakage?
    The question is not limited to PKE schemes with quantum secret keys. One can also ask
whether classical PKE schemes with classical secret keys can be secure against quantum leakage.
Of course, in this classical setting, unbounded classical leakage cannot be tolerated, since such
leakage could reveal the entire secret key. Thus, the relevant question is whether classical PKE can
tolerate bounded quantum leakage.
    To the best of our knowledge, existing works on leakage-resilient PKE consider only classical
leakage. This remains true even for post-quantum PKE schemes, which are designed to be secure
against quantum attacks. In the post-quantum setting, however, it is natural to consider adversaries
that may obtain quantum side information about the secret key. Even when the secret key is
classical, leakage is ultimately generated by a physical process. A quantum adversary may keep
this process coherent and obtain a quantum system correlated with the secret key, rather than a
measured classical outcome. Such a model may capture future settings in which devices interact
with quantum communication networks, as well as physical side channels whose leakage may be
better modeled as quantum information.
    The distinction between classical and quantum leakage is substantive. Gavinsky, Kempe,
Kerenidis, Raz, and de Wolf [GKK+ 07], building on a classical–quantum separation in communi-
cation complexity, showed that there exists a classical randomness extractor that is secure against
a certain amount of classical side information but fails in the presence of a much smaller amount
of quantum side information. This yields a direct example of a one-time symmetric-key encryption
(SKE) scheme that tolerates a certain amount of classical leakage, yet can be broken by a much
smaller amount of quantum leakage. Thus, security against classical leakage does not by itself
provide evidence of security against quantum leakage.
    This naturally motivates the following question:

Can we construct classical PKE schemes with classical secret keys that tolerate bounded quantum
                                          leakage?

1.1    Our Results
We answer these questions affirmatively. First, we extend the definition of leakage resilience for
PKE in the bounded-leakage model to allow quantum leakage. We then construct the following
two PKE schemes.

   1. A PKE scheme with quantum secret keys that is secure against unbounded clas-
      sical leakage and bounded quantum leakage. Our scheme remains secure against un-
      bounded classical leakage Lc and constant-rate bounded quantum leakage Lq . Specifically,
                                                      |Lq |
      security holds as long as the leakage ratio λ = |sk|  is at most a certain constant λ ≈ 0.057.
      Our construction relies on polynomially secure indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) and one-
      way functions (OWFs). In comparison, the prior work of [ÇGLZR24] achieved resilience only
      against unbounded classical leakage, and did so under subexponentially secure iO, subexpo-
      nentially secure OWFs, and the polynomial hardness of learning with errors (LWE). Thus, our
      result simultaneously weakens the assumptions and achieves constant-rate bounded quantum
      leakage resilience.

   2. A classical PKE scheme that is secure against bounded quantum leakage. We
      give two different instantiations of this scheme, yielding a tradeoff between assumptions and
      leakage ratio. Assuming ciphertext-policy functional encryption (CPFE) with succinct keys,
      which exists under the polynomial hardness of LWE [KN23], our scheme achieves the optimal
      leakage ratio λ = 1 − o(1). That is, the scheme remains secure even if quantum leakage of
      length almost as large as the entire secret key is leaked. Alternatively, assuming only post-
      quantum PKE, we obtain leakage ratio λ = 1/poly(n), where n is the security parameter.
      This tradeoff matches the known tradeoff in the classical-leakage setting: an optimal leakage
      ratio is achievable under LWE [BLSV18], while an inverse-polynomial leakage ratio is achiev-
      able under any PKE [HLWW16].1 Our contribution is to obtain the analogous tradeoff for
      quantum leakage in a unified framework based on CPFE. This unification is new even in the
      classical setting, and may be of independent interest.

1.2    Discussion
To motivate our work, it is natural to ask whether quantum leakage resilience follows from classical
leakage resilience.
    In the quantum secret key setting, such a separation is trivial to obtain. Start with a PKE
scheme with quantum secret keys that tolerates unbounded classical leakage, and append to its
secret key a large amount of garbage quantum state. This clearly does not affect resilience to
unbounded classical leakage. On the other hand, if the quantum secret key of the original scheme is
leaked, then the scheme is clearly insecure. If the secret-key length of the original scheme is |sk| and
                                                                                    |sk|
the length of the garbage state is ℓ, then the actual key part constitutes only a |sk|+ℓ fraction of the
secret key of the compiled scheme. Since ℓ can be chosen to be an arbitrarily large polynomial, this

leakage setting. We instead obtain the same tradeoff in a unified framework based on CPFE.

shows that unbounded classical leakage resilience does not even imply bounded quantum leakage
resilience with inverse-polynomial leakage ratio.
    The situation is more subtle in the classical secret key setting. There seems to be no trivial
example separating classical and quantum leakage resilience for PKE. As already mentioned, such
a separation is known for one-time SKE, based on [GKK+ 07]. We observe that this separation can
be lifted directly to the PKE setting in the non-adaptive leakage model, where the leakage function
cannot depend on the public key.
    The idea is as follows. Starting from any classical PKE scheme, we augment the public key
with an encryption of the PKE secret key under the above one-time SKE scheme. The secret
key of the resulting PKE scheme is then the secret key of the one-time SKE scheme. To decrypt,
one first recovers the secret key of the base PKE scheme by decrypting the additional public-key
component using the one-time SKE secret key, and then runs the decryption algorithm of the base
PKE scheme.
    In the non-adaptive leakage model, where the leakage function cannot depend on the public key,
we can rely on the classical leakage resilience of the one-time SKE scheme to prove classical leakage
resilience of the resulting PKE scheme. On the other hand, the insecurity of the one-time SKE
scheme against quantum leakage directly lifts to insecurity of the resulting PKE scheme against
quantum leakage. This gives a separation in the non-adaptive leakage model.
    Unfortunately, this idea does not work in the adaptive leakage model considered in this work.
Indeed, the above scheme is trivially insecure even against classical leakage in the adaptive leakage
model: once the public key is available, the leakage function can simply recover and output the
secret key of the base PKE scheme. Thus, we leave open the problem of separating classical and
quantum leakage resilience in the adaptive leakage model.

1.3   Related Works
Classical leakage-resilient PKE Many works have studied leakage-resilient PKE in the clas-
sical bounded-leakage model [AGV09, NS09, HLWW16, BLSV18]. In particular, prior works es-
tablish a tradeoff between assumptions and achievable leakage ratios in the classical-leakage set-
ting [HLWW16, BLSV18]. Our work gives an analogous tradeoff in the presence of quantum
leakage.
    Classical leakage-resilient PKE has also been studied in several other models, including the
bounded-retrieval model [DLW06, Dzi06, ADW09], the auxiliary-input leakage model [DKL09],
and the continual-leakage model [BKKV10, DHLW10]. Extending these models to the quantum-
leakage setting is beyond the scope of this paper and is left for future work. We refer to [KR19] for
a more extensive survey of the classical leakage-resilience literature.

PKE with quantum secret keys Considering PKE schemes with quantum secret keys as a way
to circumvent classical impossibility has recently emerged as an active line of research. The earli-
est works of this kind constructed single-decryptor encryption [GZ20, CLLZ21, LLQZ22, ÇG24b,
KY25], which enables copy-protection of secret keys. These works can be viewed as special cases
of the broader notion of quantum copy-protection [Aar09], which has also been studied extensively
in recent years [ALL+ 21, AB24, ÇG26, ABH+ 26].
    As a notion related to copy-protection, another line of work studies secure key leasing for
PKE [AKN+ 23, APV23, AHH24, KMY25], which can be viewed as an instance of the more general
concept of secure software leasing [AL21, KNY21, BJL+ 21].
    The relationship between copy-protected secret keys and unbounded classical leakage resilience
was first pointed out and studied in [ÇGLZR24]. Subsequent works extended this perspective


                                                 4
to broader primitives, such as signatures, zero-knowledge proofs, and secret sharing [ÇG24a,
CKNY25]. However, none of these works consider quantum leakage.

Quantum side information. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to study
leakage-resilient PKE against quantum leakage. More broadly, however, there is a substantial body
of work on information-theoretic security in the presence of quantum side information. This line
of work goes back at least to Renner’s framework for analyzing privacy amplification in quantum
key distribution [Ren05]. Subsequent works studied randomness extraction against quantum side
information, including the leftover hash lemma [TSSR11] and Trevisan’s extractor [DPVR12], as
well as non-malleable extractors [ACLV19, ABJO24, BJK24]. The work of Gavinsky, Kempe,
Kerenidis, Raz, and de Wolf [GKK+ 07] shows that classical and quantum side information can
behave very differently, by separating extractors secure against classical side information from
those secure against quantum side information.

Monogamy of Entanglement to LOCC Leakage We use a slightly modified version of the
MoE property of coset states, known as the Extended Monogamy of Entanglement property. This
is exactly the original MoE game defined above, except that in addition to choosing the subspace
A, the challenger also

  1. Samples a uniformly random subspace B ⊆ Fn2 of dimension 3n/4 such that A ⊂ B and a
     uniformly random subspace C ⊆ A of dimension n/4.

  2. Samples vectors v ← B and w ← C ⊥ .

Then the challenger sends descriptions of B, C, (s + v), and (t + w) along with the coset state |As,t ⟩
to A0 . It was first shown in [CLLZ21] that the MoE property of coset states implies the Extended
MoE property. The game formalizing the Extended MoE property was later defined in [ABH+ 26].
    Next, we formalize the connection between the Extended MoE property of cosets states and
cryptographic leakage. At a high level, we bound the success probability of an adversary in the
Extended MoE game, even when the adversary is additionally given arbitrary classical side infor-
mation correlated with the coset state. Following, [ÇGLZR24], we denote classical side information
correlated with a quantum secret key as leakage generated under local operations and classical
communication, or LOCC leakage.
    Previously, [ÇGLZR24] proved that the standard MoE property of coset states implies that coset
states also satisfy the standard MoE property when the adversary is also given LOCC leakage. We
call this the LOCC Leakage property of Coset States. The authors of [ÇGLZR24] formalized the
LOCC Leakage property via a leakage game between a challenger and a quantum leakage adversary,
A = (AM ain , ALeak ). The challenger sends the coset state to ALeak , who then sends a (potentially
unbounded) amount of LOCC leakage to AM ain .
    Although the standard MoE property of coset states implies the Extended MoE property, it
is not a priori clear whether the Extended MoE property suffices to establish the LOCC leakage
property. Using similar techniques to [ÇGLZR24], we show the implication indeed holds for the
Extended MoE Property of coset states. Specifically, we show that even given the additional side
information, (B, C, s + t, t + w) and LOCC leakage, the probability that (A0 , A1 , A2 ) win the MoE
game is small.

LOCC Leakage to Quantum Leakage Next, we argue coset states also satisfy the MoE
property in the presence of quantum leakage. In this model, the quantum leakage adversary
A = (AM ain , ALeak ) plays the same Extended MoE game with the challenger, except now ALeak is
allowed to output bounded quantum information as well as unbounded classical information. We
denote the quantum state output by ALeak as quantum leakage. Our proof relies on a previous
lemma proven by Boneh and Zhandry [BZ13]. At a high level, their lemma states that performing
an intermediate k-outcome partial measurement in the middle of a quantum algorithm can reduce
the probability of any fixed output by at most a factor of k.
    We use this lemma in order to prove that the Extended MoE property of coset states with
quantum leakage is implied by the Extended MoE property of coset states with LOCC leakage. In

the reduction, we simulate quantum leakage by explicitly measuring the leakage state produced by
ALeak . By the lemma, this intermediate measurement decreases the success probability of AM ain
by at most a multiplicative constant. Since the total quantum leakage is bounded by a sufficiently
small constant fraction of the secret key length, this loss is only incurs a constant factor loss in the
exponent of the success probability.

Quantum Leakage in the Computational Setting The next step in our proof is to upgrade
the established information theoretic guarantees of cosets states to the computational setting.
Looking forward, our PKE construction relies on the ability to check if a vector is in the coset A+s or
A⊥ +t. This implies that the membership checking algorithm must be public. [CLLZ21] showed that
it is indeed possible to have public coset membership by instead relying on the computational MoE
property of coset states. Their reduction assumes the existence of post-quantum indistinguishability
obfuscation and uses subspace hiding obfuscation [Zha21] in order to construct an adversary for the
information theoretic MoE property.
     In our setting, the main technical challenge is to establish that a similar reduction continues
to hold when (1) the adversary is permitted quantum leakage, and (2) we analyze the Extended
MoE property of coset states. To address this, we first formalize a version of the Extended MoE
property that is secure against computationally bounded quantum leakage adversaries. We then
prove a reduction from the information-theoretic Extended MoE property with quantum leakage
to its computational counterpart.
